coach_says: Black's knight on e4 is attacking your c3 bishop, and castling doesn't deal with it: Black just swaps on c3 and your extra pawn on e5 comes under fire. Take the knight first with Bxe4. After dxe4 the black pawn on e4 is loose, so Rd1 (hitting the queen) and then Qxe4 wins a second pawn. When an enemy piece lands on a strong central square and attacks something, ask whether trading it off leaves a weak pawn behind.
concept: trade off the strong e4 knight

coach_says: Your bishop on c4 was attacked by the knight on d6, and Ng5 ignores that. The idea of hitting f7 with knight and bishop doesn't work, because Black simply plays Nxc4 and the attack on f7 is gone; then h6 sends your knight back and Black keeps the extra pawn and the two bishops. Move the bishop first (Bb3), then win your pawn back with Re1 and Nxe5. Before launching an attack, check which of your pieces are under attack right now.

Your rook on a8 was attacked, but you had a stronger answer than blocking: Rhd8 pins the d5 bishop to White's queen on d1. If White takes Bxa8, Rxd1+ wins the queen, so White has to spend time unpinning while the bishop stays stuck. Bb7 just offers a trade and lets White off the hook. When an enemy piece sits on an open file in front of its queen, look for a rook to put on that file.
concept: pin the bishop to the queen

coach_says: Nh6+ puts your knight on the edge where White's king can attack both knights at once with Kh5. After the knight has to retreat with Ng8, Rd4+ is check (the rook can't be taken because the f6 bishop guards d4) and drives your king off d5, and then the rook takes your bishop on e4. Keep your pieces protected in the endgame and centralised: Ne5+ keeps the knight active and safe.
also: rook check forks king and bishop

coach_says: Your bishop on a7 is cut off from the game while Black's rook sits on d2 and the queen and knight eye your king. Qc7 sends your queen even further away and gets chased by R2d7, after which ...b6 boxes the a7 bishop in. Bd4 brings the bishop back to the centre and blocks the d-file between Black's rooks. When a piece has wandered off grabbing a pawn, bring it back before sending another one off.

d4 lets Black swap pieces on d4 with Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Qxd4, and then c5 and c4 come with tempo: first on your queen, then on your b3 bishop, which has to hide on a2 where it is buried behind the black pawns. Your e4 pawn also becomes a target for the b7 bishop and a rook on e8. A quiet d3 keeps your centre solid. Before opening the centre, check what the opponent's pawns can do to your bishop on b3.
concept: c5-c4 shuts in the b3 bishop

coach_says: f6 does nothing for your development, takes the best square away from your g8 knight and opens the diagonal towards your king, so after Bc4 you will struggle to castle safely. In the opening, develop a piece instead: Bf5, Nf6 or e6 all help you get castled. Pawn moves next to your king should have a real reason.

Taking on f7 was right, but with the rook. Rxf7 puts your rook on the seventh rank, where it next takes g7 and attacks Black's pawns from behind, and Bg5+ can come with check. Bxf7 only wins one pawn, and Ke7 hits the bishop so you lose time retreating it. When you can win a pawn and land a rook on the seventh rank in one move, that is usually the way.

Bxa2 grabs a pawn, but it takes your bishop off e6 and far from the action. With e6 empty, Re2 pins your e5 knight to your king, and after b3 the bishop on a2 is shut in. Bd7 keeps the bishop close and your knight and rook doing the work, and you stay clearly winning. When you are already ahead, keep your pieces together rather than sending one to the edge for a pawn.

Qb3+ is a check that helps Black: the king steps to g7, where it is safe anyway, and your queen on b3 does nothing and has to come back. You are a piece down for a pawn, so you need every move to count. b4 attacks the c5 bishop and gains time, and then Nc4 brings the knight into play. Before checking, ask what it achieves after the king steps away.

g6 leaves a hole on f6 and lets Bg5 pin your e7 knight to the queen; later the bishop can sit on f6. Ng6 is more natural: it develops the knight, frees your f8 bishop and covers the kingside. The difference is small, but when your knight on e7 is blocking your bishop, moving the knight is usually better than a pawn move.

Your queen had to move because of Nxf6+, but you could move it with a capture: f3 was attacked twice (queen and h5 bishop) and defended only once by the white queen. Qxf3 wins the pawn and offers a queen trade, taking the sting out of White's play against your king. Qg6 instead lets Rg1 hit your queen on the open g-file and White gets play. When a piece must move, check whether it can take something on the way.

Both white knights, on d5 and g4, attack f6, and only your g7 pawn defends it. White can play Ndxf6+ gxf6 Nxf6+, giving a knight for two pawns but ripping open your king, which is still in the centre and can no longer castle. Nb4 ignores that. Nxd5 removes one of the attackers. Before making your own plan, look at which of your squares the opponent is hitting twice.
concept: missed the double attack on f6

coach_says: Bh5+ drives the king to d8, but Black is happy there, and your bishop on h5 is now offside: Black's pawns and Nf6 will push it back and you end up retreating to f3 anyway. Bg3 keeps your bishop safe from g5 and gets ready to develop the queenside with Na3. Before giving a check, ask whether your piece stands better or worse after the king moves.

You wanted to attack the knights with your king, but on g5 the king can be checked by Nf7+, so Black saves the knight with tempo. Kh5 attacks the same knights from a square no knight can check; Black must retreat with Ng8 and then Rd4+ (guarded by your f6 bishop) drives the king off d5 and wins the bishop on e4. When you walk your king towards enemy knights, check every square they can jump to.
concept: king walked into a knight check
also: rook check forks king and bishop

coach_says: Good move. Bxg7 grabs a pawn and wins the h8 rook next, and you stay completely winning. Nothing to change here.
Ne4 is the best move: it hits the queen on f6 and the d6 bishop, and wins you time to trade off Black's good bishop. Well played.
g6 is fine and you stay well on top. Qf6 was even stronger, threatening Qc3+ which attacks the king and the a1 rook and c1 bishop, but you are winning either way.
Kg2 is as good as anything: your king heads to the h-file to support the g7 pawn and the win is not in danger. Nothing to fix.
Your position was already very difficult after losing material, and Qf6 is about as good as the alternatives. The damage was done earlier; there is no lesson in this particular move.
